intro: The chips I build things with, at home and at work. Ratings are my own, for embedded and drone-related work: how pleasant they are to develop for, how capable they are, and how well the ecosystem holds up.

groups.name: Microcontrollers (MCUs)
groups.blurb: Bare-metal and RTOS targets: flight controllers, sensor nodes, radios.

chips.name: STM32H7
chips.core: Arm Cortex-M7 up to 480 MHz (double-precision FPU), up to 2 MB flash, ~1 MB RAM
chips.used_for: Flight-controller firmware and bootloader work (PX4), Nucleo sensor applications
pros: The flight-controller workhorse (Pixhawk 6X/6C class)
Lots of compute and DSP headroom for estimation and control loops
Rich peripherals: FDCAN, many UARTs/SPIs, SDMMC, Ethernet
cons: Cache, MPU and DMA coherency take care to get right
Complex clock and power-domain setup
Higher power and price than mainstream parts

chips.name: STM32F4
chips.core: Arm Cortex-M4F at 168–180 MHz, up to 2 MB flash
chips.used_for: Bare-metal drivers, Zephyr projects and C++ sensor applications on the F4 Discovery
pros: Mature and extremely well documented
Huge amount of examples and community knowledge
Great for learning registers, DMA and interrupts bare-metal
cons: Showing its age next to M7/M33 parts
Limited RAM for heavier stacks
No modern security features

chips.name: STM32C5
chips.core: Arm Cortex-M33 up to 144 MHz, 128 KB–1 MB flash, up to 256 KB SRAM (launched 2026)
chips.used_for: Object-oriented security projects and Zephyr real-time projects on the NUCLEO board
pros: Cortex-M33 performance at entry-level cost
Memory protection features, TRNG and readout protection
Same STM32 tooling (CubeIDE, Zephyr) as the rest of the family
cons: Brand-new: fewer examples and community answers
Zephyr and middleware support still catching up
Peripheral set differs per variant, so check carefully

chips.name: ESP32-C6
chips.core: RISC-V HP core at 160 MHz + RISC-V LP core, 512 KB SRAM; Wi-Fi 6, BLE 5, 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee)
chips.used_for: The Home Hub behind the Live Lab page (Zephyr, HTTP server, MQTT)
pros: Wi-Fi 6, BLE and Thread/Zigbee in one cheap chip
Open RISC-V cores, good Zephyr and ESP-IDF support
Low-power core for always-on tasks
cons: Wi-Fi stack is a closed binary blob
Zephyr Wi-Fi driver still maturing
No camera interface, single application core

chips.name: ESP32 (classic)
chips.core: Dual-core Xtensa LX6 at 240 MHz, Wi-Fi + Bluetooth Classic/BLE
chips.used_for: Sensor applications, MicroPython and PlatformIO experiments, BME688 AI projects
pros: Enormous community (Arduino, MicroPython, PlatformIO)
Two cores and plenty of peripherals for the price
Fastest way from idea to a connected prototype
cons: Xtensa toolchain instead of Arm/RISC-V
Higher idle power than newer parts
Being superseded by the C- and S-series

chips.name: nRF54L15
chips.core: Arm Cortex-M33 at 128 MHz + RISC-V coprocessor, 1.5 MB NVM, 256 KB RAM; BLE, Thread, Zigbee, Matter
chips.used_for: Bluetooth Low Energy projects with Zephyr (nRF Connect SDK)
pros: Best-in-class BLE radio and low power
Zephyr is the first-class SDK
Excellent documentation and tools (nRF Connect)
cons: nRF Connect SDK has a real learning curve
Little support outside the Zephyr ecosystem
New silicon, so watch the errata

chips.name: Renesas RX140
chips.core: 32-bit RXv2 CPU at 48 MHz, low-power, capacitive touch (CTSU2)
pros: Very low active and standby current
Robust industrial-grade parts with long availability
Built-in capacitive touch sensing
cons: Proprietary RX architecture and toolchains
Small community compared to Arm parts
Zephyr support is recent

chips.name: MSP430
chips.used_for: LCD controller firmware; central-controller firmware of an encrypted USB device
pros: Microamp-level power consumption
FRAM: fast, low-power, high-endurance non-volatile memory
Simple and predictable
cons: 16-bit with limited performance and memory
Ecosystem is quieter than it used to be
Not a fit for anything compute-heavy

chips.name: ATmega328P (Arduino Uno)
chips.core: 8-bit AVR at 16 MHz, 32 KB flash, 2 KB RAM
pros: Easiest possible start
5 V I/O and tons of libraries
Great for quick hardware tests
cons: Tiny memory and performance
No on-board debugger on the Uno
Hides the low-level details a professional needs

groups.name: Application processors and SoCs (MPUs)
groups.blurb: Linux-class processors: companion computers, edge AI, gateways.

chips.name: NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX / Xavier
chips.core: Arm Cortex-A78AE cores (Orin) + Ampere GPU with tensor cores
chips.used_for: UAV companion computers, camera/LiDAR integration, Linux camera and ethernet-switch drivers
pros: The go-to drone companion computer for onboard AI
CUDA, TensorRT and a strong camera pipeline
Plenty of performance per watt for vision
cons: 10–25 W power and real thermal design needed
Kernel and Ubuntu versions tied to JetPack/L4T
Expensive modules and carriers

chips.name: NXP i.MX 8M Plus
chips.core: 4× Cortex-A53 at 1.8 GHz + Cortex-M7 at 800 MHz, 2.3 TOPS NPU, ISP, VPU
chips.used_for: FRDM-IMX8MPLUS node reporting to the Home Hub; Yocto images
pros: NPU + ISP for efficient edge vision
Real-time Cortex-M7 on the same die (RPMsg)
Long-term availability and a solid Yocto BSP
cons: Cortex-A53 cores are getting old
BSP and Yocto layers are heavy
NPU tooling (eIQ) narrower than CUDA

chips.name: Raspberry Pi (BCM2711 / BCM2712)
chips.used_for: Companion-computer prototypes, LiDAR and camera integration, C++ sensor applications
pros: Huge community and accessory ecosystem
Cheap, fast to prototype on
Good camera support
cons: Not industrial-grade; SD-card wear
Closed boot firmware and GPU
Supply and power-supply quirks

chips.name: TI AM335x (BeagleBone Black)
chips.core: Cortex-A8 at 1 GHz + 2× PRU real-time units, 512 MB RAM
chips.used_for: Kernel builds, device-tree and driver work, sensor applications
pros: PRUs give hard real-time I/O next to Linux
Open hardware with excellent documentation
Mainline kernel support, great for learning drivers
cons: Single, slow 32-bit core
Dated by today's standards
Little RAM for modern workloads

groups.name: FPGAs and adaptive SoCs
groups.blurb: Programmable logic, alone or next to hard processor cores.

chips.name: Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC
chips.used_for: Bootloader and kernel integration, systemd-based initialization, PetaLinux
pros: Linux, real-time cores and FPGA fabric on one chip
Strong security and safety features (secure boot)
Scales to very demanding I/O and acceleration
cons: Complex boot chain (FSBL, PMU, ATF, U-Boot)
Heavy tools (Vivado, PetaLinux)
Expensive parts and boards

chips.name: Zynq-7000
chips.used_for: Linux drivers for a cryptographic accelerator
pros: Classic, well-understood Linux + FPGA platform
Cheap development boards
Great for custom hardware accelerators
cons: Cortex-A9 is slow by today's standards
Same heavy toolchain as UltraScale+
Design effort for anything in the fabric

chips.name: Artix-7 (Basys3)
chips.used_for: VHDL projects, raster-scan video and register interfaces
pros: Ideal board for learning and testing VHDL
Free Vivado edition covers it
Deterministic, truly parallel logic
cons: No hard CPU; soft cores cost fabric
Limited I/O on the Basys3 board
Long build times for small changes
